doc.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: A working-class, integrated neighborhood
summary: He describes a mixed neighborhood of many languages where neighbors helped each other and the schools were integrated.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Could you describe the neighborhood you grew up in? Was it segregated, was it middle class? Oh no, this was working class neighborhood. On the corner was a farmer. His name was Mr. Strong and he was from Poland. He had horses and the plows and everything and in the spring my dad would get him to come over with the horses and the plow, and get him

to plow. We had a couple acres of land where we’d plant our garden so I always enjoyed seeing things like that. My father was so—he knew everybody. He didn’t have any bad feelings about him at all. And people do favors for him, he’d do favors for them, it was back and forth. People need a cup of sugar; he needs a cup of salt, go across the street and get it! (Laughs) They’d give it to you gladly, it was neighborhood like that. It was all kinds of people. Maybe 10 different languages.
So all the neighborhood kids, it was a pretty integrated school you went to?
Oh yes, it was all integrated. Pontiac was too small. You know you go into this one or you don’t have any school at all!
